section.title: The Resurrection and Thomas
section.sectionRationale: The dawn of the new creation. Mary finds the tomb empty, the beloved disciple sees and believes, and the risen Jesus reveals Himself to Mary in the garden, calling her by name. That evening He appears to the disciples, gives them peace and the Spirit, and sends them on mission. A week later He meets doubting Thomas, who confesses Him Lord and God. The chapter closes with John's own statement of why he wrote: that we may believe and have life.
section.thesis: The risen Jesus turns grief into joy and doubt into worship, appearing alive to Mary, to the gathered disciples whom He sends with peace and the Spirit, and to Thomas, who confesses Him Lord and God, and the whole Gospel is written so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in His name.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the empty tomb and the beloved disciple's belief; the risen Jesus and Mary in the garden; the appearance to the disciples with peace, mission, and the Spirit; the confession of Thomas; and the stated purpose of the Gospel.

verses.text: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance.
So she came running to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved. “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb,” she said, “and we do not know where they have put Him!”
Then Peter and the other disciple set out for the tomb.
The two were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.
He bent down and looked in at the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.
Simon Peter arrived just after him. He entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths lying there.
The cloth that had been around Jesus’ head was rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths.
Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in. And he saw and believed.
For they still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead.
Then the disciples returned to their homes.
But Mary stood outside the tomb weeping. And as she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb,
and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and the other at the feet.
“Woman, why are you weeping?” they asked. “Because they have taken my Lord away,” she said, “and I do not know where they have put Him.”
When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there. But she did not recognize that it was Jesus.
“Woman, why are you weeping?” Jesus asked. “Whom are you seeking?” Thinking He was the gardener, she said, “Sir, if you have carried Him off, tell me where you have put Him, and I will get Him.”
Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to Him in Hebrew, “Rabboni!” (which means “Teacher”).
“Do not cling to Me,” Jesus said, “for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go and tell My brothers, ‘I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.’”
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord!” And she told them what He had said to her.

It was the first day of the week, and that very evening, while the disciples were together with the doors locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them. “Peace be with you!” He said to them.
After He had said this, He showed them His hands and His side. The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
Again Jesus said to them, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.”
When He had said this, He breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy {{pneuma|Spirit}}.
If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld.”
Now Thomas called Didymus, one of the Twelve, was not with the disciples when Jesus came.

So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replied, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.”
Eight days later, His disciples were once again inside with the doors locked, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
Then Jesus said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.”
Thomas replied, “My Lord and my {{theos|God}}!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

units.label: The purpose of John's book
units.note: that you may believe and have life

verses.text: Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book.
But these are written so that you may {{pisteuo|believe}} that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have {{zoe|life}} in His name.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath. The risen Jesus breathes on the disciples and says, Receive the Holy Spirit, the same word for breath and Spirit. The act recalls God breathing life into Adam and points to the new creation now begun; the Spirit long promised in the farewell discourse is given to empower the sent disciples for their mission of proclaiming forgiveness.

theos.gloss: God. Thomas's cry, my Lord and my God, is the climactic confession of the Gospel, addressing the risen Jesus with the full weight of deity. It answers the prologue, the Word was God, forming a frame around the whole book: what John declared at the start, Thomas now confesses face to face before the risen Christ.

pisteuo.gloss: To believe, trust. The purpose statement names belief as the Gospel's aim: these things are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. Belief here is not bare assent but trust that receives Christ and clings to Him, the very response the whole book has been urging from its first chapter.

zoe.gloss: Life, eternal life. The final purpose of believing is that you may have life in His name. This life is the gift woven through the whole Gospel, from the life that was the light of men in the prologue to the resurrection life secured here; it is received now by faith and is the very reason John wrote.

basic.context: On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene finds the stone rolled away and runs to tell Peter and John, who race to the tomb and find it empty, the grave clothes lying there. John sees and believes. Mary, weeping, meets the risen Jesus, whom she mistakes for the gardener until He speaks her name. That evening Jesus appears to the frightened disciples behind locked doors, showing His wounds, giving them peace, sending them as the Father sent Him, and breathing on them the Spirit. Thomas, absent, refuses to believe until, a week later, Jesus meets him and Thomas cries, My Lord and my God. John then states why he wrote it all: that we may believe and have life.
basic.hermeneutics: The resurrection is the turning point of the whole story, and John gives it as eyewitness testimony. The key questions are, is Jesus truly risen, and how should we respond. The signs of the empty tomb and the appearances lead to belief; Thomas's confession, my Lord and my God, is the response the whole Gospel aims for. Note the tender personal touch, Jesus calling Mary by name, and the blessing on those who believe without seeing, which includes every later reader. The purpose statement in verse 31 is the key to the entire book.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter climbs to two great words. Jesus breathes the pneuma, the Spirit, on the disciples, echoing the breath of new creation. Thomas confesses Him theos, God, the Gospel's highest confession. And John states his purpose: that you may pisteuo, believe, and have zoe, life, in His name.
basic.typology: Jesus breathing the Spirit recalls God breathing life into Adam, marking the dawn of new creation. The garden of the resurrection answers the garden of Eden, the risen Christ mistaken for the gardener being the true gardener of the new creation. The first day of the week begins a new creation week.
basic.christ: Christ is risen, the conqueror of death, who turns grief to joy and doubt to worship. He is Lord and God, confessed by Thomas, the fulfillment of the prologue. He sends His people as the Father sent Him and gives them the Spirit.
basic.god: God the Father raised the Son and is now the Father of all who believe, for the risen Jesus calls the disciples His brothers and speaks of My Father and your Father. The resurrection vindicates the Son and opens the way into the family of God.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2 tells of God breathing life into Adam. John 1 declared the Word was God. Romans 1 says Jesus was declared Son of God by the resurrection. 1 Peter 1 speaks of the living hope through His rising.
basic.oneStory: On the first day of a new creation week, the risen Jesus steps from the tomb as the firstborn of the new creation, turning mourning into joy. He gathers and sends His people, breathes on them the Spirit, and draws even the doubter to confess Him Lord and God, so that the whole Gospel's aim is reached: that we may believe and have life in His name.

context.literary:
John 20 is built as a series of paired scenes, each running from not seeing to seeing. In the first half the two disciples run, look and leave, while Mary stays, weeps, turns and is called by name. In the second half the Lord comes to a room full of fear on the evening of the first day, and a week later He comes to the one man who was absent. Everyone in the chapter has to cross the same distance: from the absence of the body to the presence of the person. John marks the crossing with his verbs of sight. In verse 5 the beloved disciple looks in (a glance), in verse 6 Peter sees the cloths with careful observation (the verb theoreo), and in verse 8 the other disciple 'saw and believed' (the verb eido, which in John often means perceiving with understanding).

The chapter also keeps the Gospel's earlier threads in view. The linen cloths and the separate head cloth of verses 5 to 7 answer the grave clothes of Lazarus, who came out still bound, John 11:44, whereas Jesus leaves His wrappings behind, not needing anyone to unbind Him. The garden of John 19:41 becomes the setting for Mary's meeting with the one she takes for the gardener. The peace of verses 19, 21 and 26 recalls the farewell promise of John 14:27 and 16:33. And Thomas, who once said, 'let us also go, that we may die with Him,' John 11:16, now speaks the Gospel's highest confession.

Verses 30 and 31 read like the original close of the book: a statement about signs, a purpose clause, and a summary of the aim in two titles and one gift. Chapter 21 then follows as an epilogue. The shape of 20:1 to 31 is therefore a movement from a grave in the dark, 'while it was still dark,' verse 1, to a confession in the light and a book offered to the reader. The Gospel's last beatitude in verse 29 is aimed past the room, at everyone who reads.
context.historical:
A Jewish burial of the period involved wrapping the body in linen with spices, as John 19:39 and 19:40 describe, and laying it in a rock cut tomb closed by a rolled stone. Such tombs were reused, and the bones were gathered later, so an empty tomb would normally mean a stolen or moved body, which is exactly Mary's first conclusion in verse 2. Matthew 28:11 to 15 shows that the early rumour was that the disciples stole the body, so the empty tomb was not in dispute from the start; its meaning was.

All four Gospels name women as the first witnesses, and John names Mary Magdalene alone. In the first century a woman's testimony carried little weight in a courtroom. The Gospels do not tidy this embarrassment away. They report it, which is why many historians count it among the marks of authentic memory rather than invention.

The first day of the week is the day after the Sabbath. John's footnote in the BSB shows the Greek is literally 'the first of the Sabbaths,' a normal way to count days from one Sabbath to the next. That day, and the 'eight days later' of verse 26, which again falls on the first day of the week, began to shape the Christian rhythm of gathering, a pattern visible in Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2.

The doors were locked 'for fear of the Jews,' verse 19, a phrase John uses for the Jerusalem authorities who had just delivered Jesus to Pilate. The disciples knew that those who had killed the Master might come for them. Thomas was called Didymus, 'the twin,' a footnote reminds the reader, and the name is simply a Greek translation of his Aramaic one.
context.canonical:
The chapter reaches back to the beginning of the Bible. The creation week of Genesis 1 and the garden of Genesis 2 are in the background of the first day, the garden, the breathing, and the Gardener. The prophets had spoken of resurrection in terms of breath and opened graves, Ezekiel 37:1 to 14, and of dust awakening, Daniel 12:2 and Isaiah 26:19, but they had not said it would happen to one person first. John's Gospel has been preparing for it by Jesus' own words: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,' John 2:19, and 'I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again,' John 10:18.

John notes in verse 9 that the disciples 'still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead.' The Scripture in view is not named here. Luke 24:25 to 27 and 24:44 to 46 show the risen Jesus opening it up, and Peter later reads Psalm 16:10 as a promise of this resurrection in Acts 2:25 to 32. Paul states it as a tradition he received, 'raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4.

The charge of verses 21 to 23 echoes through the rest of the New Testament: Matthew 16:19 and 18:18 speak of binding and loosing, and Acts shows the apostles proclaiming forgiveness in His name, Acts 2:38 and 13:38. Thomas's confession is picked up by the Lord's own title in Revelation 1:17 and 1:18, and the last page of the Bible has the same One who showed His wounds invite the thirsty to come, Revelation 22:17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John says why he wrote, and verse 31 is the key to how he wants the whole scene read. He does not set out to prove the resurrection to a hostile courtroom; he sets out to lead readers to faith. That is why he selects. The appearances in this chapter are not a complete list, and he says so, verse 30. He picks three encounters because each one answers a different kind of person: the weeping person who needs her name spoken, the frightened group who need peace and a mission, and the sceptic who needs the evidence offered to him on his own terms.

John also wants the reader to notice a transfer. The first witnesses saw; the readers will not. Verse 29 therefore turns the scene toward everyone who comes later, and the book in the reader's hands becomes the means by which they meet the risen Lord. The author's intent is that the reader stands in Thomas's place and says what Thomas said.

There is also a quiet argument in how the story is told. The beloved disciple believes before he has seen the Lord, from the cloths alone, verse 8, so faith is shown beginning in the evidence of the empty tomb and the order within it. Mary and Thomas show faith beginning in a personal encounter. John allows both paths and offers both to his readers.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what happened on particular days to particular people. It does not command believers to demand the kind of proof Thomas asked for, and Jesus' answer is not a standing offer of the same sign to every doubter. Verse 29 tells us how He regards Thomas's route compared with the way of those who come to faith without having seen. It is gentle toward Thomas and blessing toward the rest.

The charge of verses 22 and 23 is often misread as describing a priestly power exercised in a ritual. The text addresses the gathered disciples with the Spirit just given, and the pattern Acts shows is the declaration of forgiveness through the gospel message, not a private act of any one person. The commission applies to the church as it carries the message of Christ, and the Spirit remains its power. It prescribes mission, not a special privilege.

What carries forward directly is the peace, the sending, the breath of the Spirit, and the invitation to believe on the strength of a written testimony.

debates.question: What did Jesus mean by 'Do not cling to Me' to Mary?

views.label: Stop holding on, because the relationship is changing
views.case: The Greek is a present imperative with a negative, which many take as 'stop clinging.' Mary's grasp is the clutch of someone who thinks she has her old Teacher back. Jesus says He has not yet ascended, so the relationship she must learn is the one that comes after His going to the Father, a relationship of the Spirit rather than of physical presence.

views.label: Do not hold Me, for the ascension is still ahead
views.case: Others read the verse as a reassurance rather than a rebuke: she does not need to hold on, because He is not leaving for good in that moment. He will go to the Father, and her task is to go and tell the brothers. On this reading the point is her mission, not her fault.

views.label: A puzzle with Thomas
views.case: Because Jesus invites Thomas to touch His wounds in verse 27, some feel a tension that needs resolving. The two situations differ. Mary is told not to remain holding Him, while Thomas is offered touch as evidence. The text itself says that Thomas is invited to see and touch, and does not say whether he actually did.

debates.bearing: On every reading the emphasis falls on what follows: the new relationship with the Father, 'My Father and your Father,' and the errand to the brothers. Mary is given a task instead of a grip.

debates.question: What is given in the breathing of verse 22, and how does it relate to Pentecost?

views.label: A first giving of the Spirit, with Pentecost as the public outpouring
views.case: The breath is a real impartation to the apostles, and Acts 2 is the wider, public arrival of the Spirit with power. Luke places the promised baptism of Acts 1:5 before Pentecost, not at the evening of Easter, and John's gift prepares for it.

views.label: A symbolic anticipation
views.case: Others take the breathing as an acted promise that points ahead to Pentecost. In John 7:39 the Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified, and in John 16:7 He must go away for the Helper to come. On this view the breathing is a pledge, not yet the fulfilment.

views.label: John's Pentecost
views.case: Some hold that John and Luke tell the same giving from different angles, John in the closed room for the leaders and Luke in the public square for the nations. The Gospels do not claim to be harmonised on this.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the Spirit comes from the risen Lord, that He comes in the context of sending, and that the gift is for mission as much as comfort.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 22 says that Jesus 'breathed on them,' using a verb that is rare in the New Testament. It is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7, where God breathed the breath of life into the man, and again in Ezekiel 37:9, where the prophet calls the breath to breathe into the slain so that they may live. John does not explain the echo. He lets it stand: the same Creator who made a living being from dust now makes a new community from frightened disciples.

The sending of verse 21 uses two verbs. 'As the Father has sent Me' uses apostello, and 'I am sending you' uses pempo. Some have tried to make a sharp distinction between them. Within John the two verbs are used of the Father's sending of the Son with no clear difference, so the point is not a ranking of missions but the pattern: the disciples' sending is modelled on the Father's sending of the Son, with the same authority and the same dependence.

In verse 23 the first verb, 'forgive,' is aphiemi, and the second, 'withhold,' is krateo, which means to hold fast or retain. The first is in a form that many read as 'have been forgiven,' a completed state; and a number of interpreters take it to mean that the church announces a forgiveness already settled in heaven, rather than creating it.

The phrase translated 'Stop doubting and believe' in verse 27 is literally 'do not be unbelieving but believing,' using the adjectives apistos and pistos. John does not call Thomas a doubter in the modern sense of one who weighs evidence; he calls him to move out of unbelief into belief, and the same stem pistos, faith, runs through the whole chapter and ends in verse 31.

Thomas says, 'I will never believe,' and the Greek doubles the negative, ou me, an emphatic denial of any possibility. His later words, ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou, use the article and the nominative where a vocative address would be expected. The effect is a direct address with the force of a declaration: 'the Lord of me and the God of me.'

The footnote on verse 31 notes that some manuscripts have a present tense for 'believe,' which would mean 'that you may continue to believe,' while others have a form that could mean 'that you may come to believe.' The manuscripts are divided, and both aims fit the Gospel: it wins faith and keeps it.

Mary answers in Hebrew with 'Rabboni,' and the footnote notes the language may be Aramaic. It is the same form the blind man uses in Mark 10:51. John translates it as 'Teacher,' which is a gentle, personal form of the title 'Rabbi' used elsewhere in the Gospel. A grieving woman reaches for the mother tongue.

typology.type: The first day and the new creation week
typology.fulfillment: The Gospel opens, 'In the beginning,' John 1:1, and John now marks 'the first day of the week,' verse 1, for the dawn. A new creation begins on the first day, with a garden, a man who breathes life, and a woman who meets her Maker. Creation began with light on the first day, Genesis 1:3 to 5; the new creation begins with the dark of the tomb giving way to the light of Easter. The pattern is cosmic, not only personal, since Paul says 'if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation,' 2 Corinthians 5:17. The type falls short in that the first creation was spoken, while this one is won through a death.

typology.type: The sheaf of firstfruits waved on the day after the Sabbath
typology.fulfillment: Leviticus 23:10 and 11 commanded that a sheaf of the first harvest be waved before the LORD on the day after the Sabbath, as a pledge of the full harvest to come. Jesus rises on exactly that day, and Paul calls Him 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. What the sheaf promised, a harvest following, is what His rising guarantees for His people, 1 Corinthians 15:23. The type falls short in scale: the sheaf was grain, while the harvest of Christ's rising is a people raised in bodies like His glorious body, Philippians 3:21.

typology.type: The breath of life in Adam and the breath on the valley of bones
typology.fulfillment: God breathed into Adam's nostrils and he became a living being, Genesis 2:7, and Ezekiel was told to call the breath into dead bones that they might live, Ezekiel 37:9. In John 20:22 the risen Lord breathes on His disciples and gives the Holy Spirit. The correspondence is deliberate, since Jesus is the Creator and the one who sends the Spirit. The escalation is that the breath is now His own, and Paul calls the risen Christ 'a life-giving spirit,' 1 Corinthians 15:45. The type falls short because Adam's breath gave natural life, while Christ's breath gives the life of the age to come.

typology.type: The garden and the true Gardener
typology.fulfillment: Jesus is buried in a garden, John 19:41, and Mary mistakes Him for the gardener, verse 15. John does not state the connection, but readers who know Genesis hear it. In the first garden the man was set to work and keep it, and a woman and a man hid from God after the fall, Genesis 3:8. In this garden a woman looks for the dead and finds the living Lord, who calls her by name. The fuller picture is Revelation 22:1 and 2, where the river and the tree of life are restored. The type is suggestive more than formal, and John's words are a mistaken guess that carries a deeper truth.

study.christ:
The Gospel began with the Word who was God, John 1:1, and it now closes its main narrative with a man saying exactly that to the risen Jesus. Thomas's confession draws the prologue's claim to a point, and Jesus does not correct him. In a Gospel where the Jews sought to kill Him for making Himself equal with God, John 5:18, His acceptance of 'My Lord and my God' is deliberate. Others in the New Testament refuse worship, Acts 10:25 and 26 and Revelation 22:8 and 9. He receives it.

The resurrection also reveals what kind of Lord this is. He comes to the locked room through the fear rather than going around it, and His first word is peace. He shows His wounds, so that the glorified body is identified by the marks of the cross. The wounds are not hidden as an embarrassment. They are the credentials of the one who laid down His life, John 10:17 and 18, and they are the reason the disciples rejoice. The Lamb who was slain is the one who lives, Revelation 5:6.

He calls Mary by name, which is how the Good Shepherd was said to treat His sheep, 'He calls His own sheep by name,' John 10:3, and 'My sheep listen to My voice,' John 10:27. The resurrection is not only a doctrine but a personal recognition. And He calls the disciples 'My brothers,' verse 17, which the book of Hebrews reads with the Psalm that says 'I will proclaim Your name to My brothers,' Hebrews 2:11 and 12, quoting Psalm 22:22. The one who has defeated death is not ashamed to call us family.

Finally, Christ is the giver of the Spirit. The breath of the new creation belongs to the risen Lord, and the sending of verse 21 makes the church an extension of His mission, so the Christ of John 20 is the Lord who rules, the God who is worshipped, and the Shepherd who knows His own by name.
study.god:
The chapter shows the Father in the words of the Son: 'My Father and your Father, to My God and your God,' verse 17. The sentence holds together what Jesus uniquely is and what He gives to His people. He does not say 'our Father,' as though He and the disciples stood in the same relation. He says 'My Father and your Father,' keeping both the distinction and the gift. The Father of the eternal Son has become, through the death and resurrection of the Son, the Father of those who believe. It is the plainest statement in John that adoption flows from the cross and the empty tomb.

The chapter also shows the Trinity at work. The Father sends, the Son sends in His turn, and the Spirit is breathed on the church, verse 21 and 22. This is not an abstract doctrine but a mission. God the Father's love for the world, John 3:16, becomes the sending of the Son; the Son sends His people, and the Spirit equips them. Worship in this light is not retreat but response to the Father's initiative.

God is shown as patient with doubt. He does not leave Thomas in his unbelief for a week without meeting him, and when He comes He speaks Thomas's own words back to him, verse 27. The same God who is worshipped as Lord and God stoops to a sceptic's conditions. The tenderness of God is joined with the sovereignty of the risen Christ.

The chapter also holds together God's timing and human delay. Mary's grief, the disciples' fear, and Thomas's absence all pass through hours and days, yet the resurrection happens when the Father determined. The God of John 20 is not hurried by sorrow, but He is not distant from it either. Worship in this chapter begins in the middle of tears and ends in confession: 'My Lord and my God.'

crossReferences.note: Lazarus came out of his tomb still wrapped in strips of linen with his face covered, and others had to unbind him. Jesus leaves His wrappings behind and the head cloth rolled up and lying separate, which shows a different kind of rising: Lazarus returned to a life that would end again, while Jesus rose beyond death's reach.

God formed the man from the dust and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. John 20:22 uses the same Greek verb for breathing in the Septuagint, so the risen Lord is shown doing what the Creator did at the first, now for a community instead of a single man.

The prophet is told to call the breath into the slain so that they may live. The vision of a restored people is answered here when the risen Lord breathes the Spirit on His disciples, who had been as good as dead in their locked room, and sends them out alive.

The Shepherd calls His own sheep by name and they know His voice. At the tomb the stranger she takes for the gardener says one word, 'Mary,' and she knows Him at once. Recognition comes through being known and called, not through sight.

Peter vowed to lay down his life for Him. The room of locked doors in chapter 20 shows how that boast ended. The restoration of the same group, by peace and a commission, is grace that the farewell night had promised: 'you will follow later.'

Jesus said, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,' and John later explains that He meant the temple of His body. The empty tomb is the fulfilment of that first public claim, and so the disciples' later memory of His words gives the resurrection its meaning.

David says God will not abandon his soul to the grave or let His Holy One see decay. Peter uses this in Acts 2:27 and 31 to show that the prophecy could not have been about David, who died and was buried, but about the Christ whom God raised.

Paul records the early list of those to whom the risen Christ appeared, including Cephas and the Twelve, over five hundred at once, and James. This is the testimony that stands beside John's selection, and shows that his chosen scenes were part of a wider witness known to the church.

The risen Lord claims all authority and sends His disciples to all nations with the promise that He will be with them to the end of the age. John 20:21 is the same commissioning in the Gospel's own words, with the Spirit given as the means of the presence that Matthew promises.

The one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified come from one source, and so He is not ashamed to call them brothers. John 20:17 is where the word first sounds, spoken on Easter morning to a weeping woman who is told to carry it to the others.

study.oneStory:
The story began with a good creation and a human pair who were told that disobedience would bring death, Genesis 2:17. Death came, and with it the long sorrow that Genesis 5 recites in its refrain, 'and then he died.' Everything from that point was moving toward the answer, and the Old Testament held its hope in pieces: the promise of the seed who would crush the serpent, Genesis 3:15, the sacrifices that covered but did not remove, the prophets who spoke of a people raised and a death swallowed up, Isaiah 25:8.

John 20 is where those pieces meet. On the first day of the week, in a garden, the Lord of creation walks out of death alive, the first of a new humanity, and in the evening He breathes the breath of the new age on His people. The Spirit that was only promised in the prophets, Ezekiel 36:26 and 27 and Joel 2:28, is now given by the risen Lord, and He sends His church in the same way the Father sent Him. The Gospel's own purpose is the story's purpose: that people from every nation may believe and have life in His name.

What waits ahead is the full harvest. The firstfruits has been waved. Paul says that the last enemy to be destroyed is death, 1 Corinthians 15:26, and John himself sees the end in which God wipes away every tear and 'there will be no more death,' Revelation 21:4. Thomas's confession will then be the confession of every tongue. The risen Jesus of John 20 stands between the garden of loss and the garden city of Revelation 22, and He is the pledge that the story ends in life.

quiz.q: How does Jesus reveal Himself to the weeping Mary at the tomb?

options.text: He calls her by name, and she recognizes Him.
options.note: Verse 16 shows the personal recognition when Jesus says, Mary.

options.text: He shows her His wounds so she will know Him.
options.note: He shows His wounds to the disciples later; to Mary, recognition comes simply when He speaks her name.

options.text: He appears in blinding glory that overwhelms her.
options.note: He appears as the risen Lord and calls her name; there is no overwhelming display.

options.text: He speaks to her and she knows His voice.
options.note: True, but it omits the tender detail that He calls her by name, Mary.

quiz.q: What does Jesus give the disciples when He appears to them that evening?

options.text: Peace, a mission as the Father sent Him, and the Holy Spirit.
options.note: Verses 19 to 22 give peace, sending, and the Spirit.

options.text: Reassurance by showing them His wounds.
options.note: He does show His hands and side, but He also gives them peace, a mission, and the Spirit.

options.text: Only a brief greeting before leaving.
options.note: He gives them peace, commission, and the Spirit, far more than a greeting.

options.text: Peace and a commission to go out.
options.note: True, but it omits the breathing of the Holy Spirit on them.

quiz.q: How does Thomas respond when Jesus meets him?

options.text: He confesses, My Lord and my God.
options.note: Verse 28 records the Gospel's climactic confession of Christ's deity.

options.text: He still refuses to believe.
options.note: He believes and makes the highest confession in the Gospel.

options.text: He simply says he is sorry for doubting.
options.note: He does more than apologize; he worships Jesus as Lord and God.

options.text: He acknowledges that Jesus is truly risen.
options.note: True, but it falls short of his actual confession of Jesus as Lord and God.

quiz.q: What blessing does Jesus pronounce after Thomas believes?

options.text: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.
options.note: Verse 29 extends the blessing to all later believers who trust the testimony.

options.text: Blessed are those who believe once they have seen.
options.note: Those who see and believe, like Thomas, are not cursed, but the special blessing rests on those who believe without seeing.

options.text: Blessed are only those who saw Him in person.
options.note: The blessing reaches especially those who believe without seeing.

options.text: Blessed are those who come to faith through the witness of others.
options.note: True in effect, but it does not capture the exact wording, those who have not seen and yet have believed.

quiz.q: Why did John write his Gospel, according to verse 31?

options.text: So that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in His name.
options.note: Verse 31 states the Gospel's purpose plainly.

options.text: To record the most important signs Jesus did.
options.note: He recorded selected signs, but the stated purpose is not mere record; it is that readers believe and have life.

options.text: To settle debates among scholars.
options.note: The stated purpose is belief and life, not academic debate.

options.text: So that readers may know who Jesus is.
options.note: True but incomplete; the goal is not only knowledge but believing faith that brings life in His name.

questions: Jesus turned Mary's grief to joy by speaking her name. How does it change your view of the risen Christ to know He calls you personally?
The disciples were hiding in fear when Jesus came with peace. Where do you need the risen Lord to meet you in your fear with His peace?
Jesus sent the disciples as the Father sent Him, and gave them His Spirit. How are you living as one sent by the risen Christ, empowered by the Spirit?
Thomas moved from doubt to the confession, my Lord and my God. How does Jesus meet your doubts, and is that confession truly your own?
John wrote so that you may believe and have life. Have you received the life he points to, and how might your life show that you truly believe?

translationNotes.note: Early on the first day of the week; the BSB footnote gives the literal on the first of the Sabbaths. The resurrection on the first day inaugurated the Christian Lord's Day.
Rabboni, which John translates Teacher, is an Aramaic term of deep respect; the BSB footnote notes it may be Aramaic. Mary's recognition comes when Jesus speaks her name.
He breathed on them and said, Receive the Holy Spirit; the same word means breath and Spirit, echoing God breathing life into Adam in Genesis 2:7.
So that you may believe; the BSB footnote notes some manuscripts read may continue to believe. Either way the aim is faith that brings life in Christ's name.
